title: What is a database index, and why does it make reads faster?
tldr: An index is an ordered structure (usually a B-tree) enabling O(log n) lookups instead of an O(n) sequential scan, at the cost of write overhead and storage.

title: How does a B-tree index actually work internally?
tldr: A B-tree's shallow, multi-key nodes keep lookups O(log n); leaf nodes are sorted and linked, which is also why B-trees serve range queries well and hash indexes can't.

title: How does column order matter in a composite (multicolumn) index?
tldr: A composite index only helps queries that constrain a leftmost-contiguous prefix of its columns — a condition on a non-leading column alone can't narrow the scan.

title: What is a covering index / index-only scan?
tldr: An index-only scan answers a query entirely from the index (skipping the heap) when every needed column is present in the index, e.g. via a covering INCLUDE index.

title: How do you read an `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output to find a bad plan?
tldr: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows planned vs. actual cost/rows per node — look for seq scans on large tables, big estimate/actual gaps, Filter vs Index Cond, and I/O buffer stats to find the bottleneck node.

title: How do you find your worst-performing queries in a live production database?
tldr: Use aggregate tooling like pg_stat_statements (or MySQL's slow query log) sorted by total/mean exec time to find real offenders, then drill in with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and correlate with app-level tracing.

title: Why do stale table statistics cause bad query plans?
tldr: Query plans are estimates built from statistics gathered by ANALYZE — if data shifts since the last ANALYZE, estimates go stale and the planner can pick a much worse plan.

title: What is MVCC, and why does it mean readers don't block writers?
tldr: MVCC keeps old row versions visible to in-flight transactions instead of blocking readers, so reads and writes never block each other — at the cost of dead-tuple bloat needing VACUUM.

title: Walk through PostgreSQL's row-level lock modes and how `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` affects concurrency.
tldr: FOR UPDATE takes an exclusive row lock (blocks all other lockers), FOR SHARE takes a shared one (blocks writers only) — overusing FOR UPDATE serializes work and can cause deadlocks.

title: Why is an index lookup O(log n) and a full scan O(n) — and when does that stop mattering?
tldr: Index lookups are O(log n) vs. a scan's O(n), but that edge shrinks or reverses at low selectivity, where random index-to-heap I/O can cost more than one cheap sequential pass.

title: What real-world problem do indexes solve, and what did databases do before them?
tldr: Indexes trade a small ongoing write cost for near-constant-time reads, avoiding the linear scan cost that would otherwise grow with table size — the same precompute-to-avoid-repeated-work trade-off as caching.

title: What's the risk of over-indexing a table?
tldr: Every index adds real write, storage, and planner-overhead costs — index deliberately based on actual query patterns and periodically prune unused ones via pg_stat_user_indexes.

title: Why does wrapping an indexed column in a function or implicit cast stop the index from being used?
tldr: Wrapping an indexed column in a function or implicit cast makes the condition non-sargable, forcing a scan; fix by rewriting to a raw-column range condition or building a matching expression index.

title: What's a partial index, and when would you use one?
tldr: A partial index only covers rows matching a predicate, saving space/write cost when queries consistently target a skewed subset — also useful for enforcing a unique constraint on that subset.

title: B-tree vs. Hash index — what's the actual trade-off?
tldr: B-tree supports equality, ranges, and sorting; hash indexes support only equality and can't produce sorted output, since hashing deliberately destroys key ordering.

title: What's the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered (secondary) index?
tldr: In InnoDB the primary key IS the table's physical storage (clustered index); every secondary index stores the primary key instead of a row pointer, making secondary lookups a two-step bookmark hop.

title: What is parameter sniffing, and how does it cause a query to suddenly get slow?
tldr: Parameter sniffing caches a plan built from the first execution's parameter values, so if that value was atypical, every later call reuses a plan optimized for the wrong data shape until it's evicted.

title: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you detect and fix it?
tldr: The N+1 problem is one query per parent row from a lazily-loaded relation accessed in a loop; fix with eager fetching (JOIN FETCH) so the related data comes back in one query instead of N extra ones.

title: Why does PostgreSQL need `VACUUM`, and how does bloat degrade performance?
tldr: MVCC leaves dead tuples behind after UPDATE/DELETE; unreclaimed dead tuples bloat tables/indexes and slow scans — VACUUM (usually via autovacuum) reclaims that space.

title: How do transaction isolation levels trade correctness for concurrency/performance?
tldr: Stronger isolation levels (Repeatable Read, Serializable) prevent more concurrency anomalies but cost more contention/aborts — Read Committed is the default because it's correct enough for most operations at the best concurrency.
